cues.text: A Deacon of the Roman Church
Lawrence served as one of the seven deacons of Rome under Pope Sixtus II .
According to the ancient office of the diaconate, he was entrusted with the care of the Church's material goods and, above all, with the distribution of alms to the city's poor, widows, and orphans.
It was a position of real responsibility in a Roman Church that, though still officially outlawed, had grown considerable in size and in charity.
When the persecution of the Emperor Valerian struck in the summer of 258, it fell first and hardest upon the Church's leadership.
Sixtus and several of his deacons were seized and beheaded almost at once, while presiding, according to a treasured tradition, at the very altar.
The Treasures of the Church
Lawrence alone among the deacons was spared for a few more days, for the Roman prefect, assuming the Church held vast wealth, demanded that Lawrence surrender its treasures to the imperial treasury.
Lawrence asked for three days to gather them together.
He used the time not to hide gold, but to distribute whatever funds remained in his keeping among the city’s poor.
Nothing material was left to hand over.
On the appointed day, he returned before the prefect, leading a great procession of Rome’s blind, lame, sick, and destitute.
In words the Church has treasured ever since, he declared that these — the poor whom Christ himself called blessed — were the true and only treasures of the Church.
A Martyrdom Remembered With Awe
Furious at what he took for defiance, the prefect condemned Lawrence to a particularly cruel death: to be burned alive upon an iron grate set over slow coals.
St. Ambrose of Milan , writing little more than a century later, already knew and passed on the tradition of Lawrence's extraordinary composure in this trial.
His serenity was so total that later writers, above all the poet Prudentius, added the detail that Lawrence bid his executioners simply to turn him over, since one side, he said, was cooked enough.
The faithful have cherished that detail ever since, even where historians urge caution.
Whatever we make of this famous detail, the substance beneath it was accepted without question by the Church of the very next generation.
That substance was a deacon of Rome facing an agonizing death with unshaken peace.
It is this deeper truth, rather than any single dramatic phrase, that the centuries have rightly cherished.
Rome's Own Martyr
Lawrence's death made an impression on the city of Rome unlike almost any other martyrdom of the age.
Once Christianity had been granted peace, Constantine himself raised an oratory over Lawrence's burial place on the Via Tiburtina.
Pope Sixtus III later built there a great basilica, San Lorenzo fuori le Mura, which stands to this day among Rome's seven principal churches.
It has been a place of pilgrimage without interruption for over a thousand years.
His feast, kept on the tenth of August, has been observed continuously since at least the year 354.
It is among the oldest unbroken feast days of the entire Christian calendar, a testament to how quickly and how deeply this one deacon's courage took hold of the Roman imagination.
Legacy
Lawrence stands before every generation of the Church as a reminder of something the world is always tempted to forget.
The true wealth of the Christian community has never been gold or silver, vestments or buildings, but the poor and suffering members of Christ's own Body, in whom he himself is present and hidden.
In a world still measuring worth by what can be counted and possessed, Lawrence answered the Roman prefect: these are the treasures of the Church .
His answer remains as sharp and necessary today as it was in the searing summer of 258.
